name: BloodHound.py - Remote AD Data Collection (Linux)
description: Python-based BloodHound data collector — runs from a Linux attack host without needing to touch the target Windows environment beyond LDAP/SMB queries. Collects users, groups, computers, GPOs, sessions, ACLs, trusts, and local admin relationships. Output is JSON files ready for import into BloodHound/Neo4j.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== BLOODHOUND OVERVIEW ===
BloodHound uses graph theory to visualize AD attack paths. It collects raw data
(users, groups, ACLs, sessions, trusts) and stores it in a Neo4j graph database.
The GUI then lets you run pre-built queries like:
  'Shortest path to Domain Admins from <your user>'
  'Find all Kerberoastable users'
  'Find DCSync rights'
  'Who can RDP anywhere?'

=== COLLECTION METHODS (-c flag) ===
  All          → collect EVERYTHING (recommended for exams/assessments)
  Default      → basic collection (users, groups, trusts, ACLs)
  Session      → only who is logged on where (requires admin on targets)
  LocalAdmin   → local group membership (requires admin on targets)
  DCOM,RDP,PSRemote → specific remote access rights
  LoggedOn     → sessions visible without admin (from LDAP; less complete)

=== WHAT IT QUERIES ===
  - LDAP port 389/636 → users, groups, OUs, GPOs, ACLs, trusts
  - SMB port 445 → local admin membership, sessions (for Session/LocalAdmin)
  Note: -c All includes session enumeration which touches every live machine —
  louder, but more complete picture.

=== OUTPUT FILES ===
bloodhound-python creates a ZIP or individual JSON files:
  20231015_computers.json
  20231015_users.json
  20231015_groups.json
  20231015_gpos.json
  20231015_ous.json
  20231015_domains.json
Import ALL of them into BloodHound at once via drag-and-drop.

=== COMMON ISSUES ===
  Name resolution errors → add DC IP to /etc/hosts
  'Cannot find domain' → specify -ns <dc_ip> explicitly
  Session data empty → need admin access for full session enum
  Timeout → reduce scope with -c Default instead of All

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: bloodhound-python is the Linux BloodHound collector, gathering the same graph data over LDAP/SMB without a Windows host.
defense.prerequisites: Valid domain credentials and network access to the DC from Linux.
defense.impact: The full BloodHound attack-path graph, collected from Linux.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1087.002] bulk LDAP queries (4662 / Defender for Identity) and SMB enumeration from one source; the JSON/zip output.
defense.artifacts: Collected JSON/zip; mass LDAP + SMB queries.
defense.prevention: Defender for Identity recon detection; LDAP anomaly monitoring; least privilege.
defense.evasion: Collect only needed methods (--collectionmethod) and throttle to reduce the query burst.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects
